academy.title: Academy
academy.intro: Eleven short chapters that explain every system of the game with its real rules and numbers. Read them in order or jump to any chapter; you can come back at any time, also during a game with the ? buttons in the ministries.
academy.start.title: Getting Started
academy.start.1.title: Starting a game
academy.start.1.body:
From the main menu choose New Game → Modern World. Three steps follow:

• AI aggressiveness: Peaceful, Realistic, Aggressive or Chaos. It decides how often the other countries sanction, threaten, declare war and join wars, and how much stronger they want to be before they attack.
• Your country: pick it on the map or from the list (search by name). Larger, richer countries are easier; small or unstable ones are harder.
• Your leader's name.

The game starts on the scenario date with real data: GDP, debt, armies, alliances and wars of today.
academy.start.2.title: Controls on phone and PC
academy.start.2.body:
• Move the map: drag with one finger or the mouse.
• Zoom: pinch with two fingers, or use the mouse wheel.
• Open a province: tap or click it. Its card (dossier) shows the owner, people, cities, armies and buildings.
• Select several cities on a PC: hold Shift and click, or hold Shift and drag a box over the map.
• Close a panel: the × in its top corner, or tap outside a dialog.
academy.start.3.title: The top bar
academy.start.3.body:
Everything important about your country is in the top bar, and every block opens its ministry:

• Flag with your world rank (#1 is the strongest country; the top 8 are great powers) → rankings.
• Treasury, GDP and inflation → Ministry of Finance.
• Support → Ministry of the Interior.
• Army → Ministry of Defence.
• Dipl. (diplomatic points) → Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
• The light bulb → Technology (the badge shows points waiting to be assigned).
• The podium → world rankings. Menu → save, load, goals, settings, exit.
academy.start.4.title: Turns: one turn is one week
academy.start.4.body:
The game is turn-based. You give orders, then press Next Turn (bottom right). One turn is one week. The world then moves in a fixed order: AI decisions, missile hits, movement, battles, construction and training, the economy, the population, diplomacy, events, and finally an autosave.

All durations in the game are in weeks: construction, training, ultimatum deadlines, assimilation. A missile launched this week hits next week, wherever the target is.
academy.start.5.title: Map modes, news and reports
academy.start.5.body:
The button at the bottom left (Political ▾) switches map modes: political, support, relations, alliances, resources and air defense. Use them to see at a glance where people are angry, who likes you and who is protected.

The WIRE strip at the bottom shows world news. Ministers send urgent messages (war declared on you, an ultimatum, a strike, riots). Every 10 weeks the cabinet sends a general report: GDP, budget, support, wars, sanctions and the biggest changes in relations.
academy.economy.title: National Economy
academy.economy.1.title: The Ministry of Finance
academy.economy.1.body: Tap the treasury, GDP and inflation block in the top bar. The Ministry of Finance shows your GDP and its yearly growth, treasury, debt, inflation, the weekly budget line by line, the controls (taxes, public services, research, money printing, foreign investment policy), your construction projects and charts of your history (GDP, treasury, support, provinces, technology, rank).
academy.economy.2.title: The weekly budget
academy.economy.2.body:
Each week the budget is: income − expenses = balance.

Income:

• Taxes: GDP × tax rate ÷ 52, lowered when provinces riot or are not assimilated, raised by technology.
• Investments abroad: returns from buildings you own in other countries.
• Trade: your treasury's share of resource exports.

Expenses:

• Military: what your soldiers cost (less with technology).
• Public services: GDP × services share ÷ 52.
• Debt interest, building upkeep and research.
academy.economy.3.title: Surplus, deficit, treasury and debt
academy.economy.3.body:
A positive balance (surplus) adds to the treasury every week. A negative balance (deficit) is paid from the treasury; when the treasury cannot cover it, the rest becomes debt.

Debt costs interest: {interestRate}% a year, plus more the higher the debt is compared with GDP. Above {debtThreshold}% of GDP, debt also slows growth, and a heavy debt lowers public support.

Example: with a deficit of $50 m a week and $1 bn in the treasury, the money lasts 20 weeks; after that every week adds $50 m of debt.
academy.economy.4.title: GDP and growth
academy.economy.4.body:
GDP is the size of your economy, and most of the game is built on it: taxes, services and research are shares of GDP, and so are many diplomatic weights.

Growth starts from {baseGrowth}% a year and changes with:

• Taxes above {taxThreshold}% slow growth.
• Public services above {servicesNeutral}% of GDP speed it up; below, they slow it down.
• Inflation above {inflationThreshold}% slows growth.
• Debt above {debtThreshold}% of GDP slows it.
• Technology (economic growth category) adds to it.

Growth stays between {minGrowth}% and {maxGrowth}% a year. Finished buildings add GDP directly.
academy.economy.5.title: Inflation and printing money
academy.economy.5.body:
Inflation moves slowly toward a target each week. The target starts at about {inflationBase}% and rises when:

• the deficit is larger than {deficitThreshold}% of GDP a year,
• total spending is above {spendingThreshold}% of GDP,
• you print money.

Print money gives the treasury instant cash ({printShare}% of GDP each time) but pushes inflation up, and the printed money keeps pushing for a while. High inflation slows growth and costs public support. The Minister of Finance warns you when inflation passes {inflationAlert}%.

Use printing only in an emergency, for example to pay an army during a war.
academy.economy.6.title: Foreign investment and trade
academy.economy.6.body:
You can build in other countries' cities if they agree (rivals and enemies refuse). The host gets the GDP; you pay the cost and receive {foreignReturn}% of it a year as returns. Returns stop while you are at war with the host or one of you sanctions the other.

In the Ministry of Finance you can also refuse all foreign investment in your country (Reject all); your own investments still work.

Resources (oil, gas, food, chips and others) are traded automatically between partner countries; the Resources map mode shows them. A shortage, for example of food, lowers support; a lack of chips stops weapons factories.
academy.taxes.title: Taxes and Public Services
academy.taxes.1.title: The tax rate
academy.taxes.1.body:
The tax rate is a slider in the Ministry of Finance, from {taxMin}% to {taxMax}% of GDP. Countries start with their real level ({startTax}% where no data exists).

• Higher taxes → more income every week.
• Above {taxThreshold}% they slow GDP growth and lower public support in every province.

Example: on a $100 bn GDP, each extra percentage point of tax brings about $19 m a week.
academy.taxes.2.title: Public services
academy.taxes.2.body:
Public services (health, schools, police, administration) are a share of GDP, from {servicesMin}% to {servicesMax}%. They are an expense, but:

• above {servicesNeutral}% of GDP they raise growth and public support,
• below {servicesNeutral}% they lower both.

The administration technology category makes the same services cheaper.
academy.taxes.3.title: Research
academy.taxes.3.body: Research is the third slider: 0–{researchMax}% of GDP (most countries start near {researchStart}%). It is an expense that raises your technology level over time; every new level gives {pointsPerLevel} technology points. See Advanced Gameplay for the technology categories.
academy.taxes.4.title: Finding the balance
academy.taxes.4.body:
Taxes and services pull in opposite directions: taxes fill the treasury but anger people, services cost money but calm them and grow the economy. Changes apply from the next week, and support moves toward its new level gradually.

A safe start: keep taxes near {taxThreshold}% and services near {servicesNeutral}%, then adjust while watching the weekly balance, inflation and support. If support falls toward {riotThreshold}%, lower taxes or raise services before riots begin.
academy.population.title: Population and Workforce
academy.population.1.title: Provinces, cities and people
academy.population.1.body: Every province has people living in its cities and the countryside, and a culture (the people who live there). Open a province to see its population, cities and status. Population decides how much a province produces and how many soldiers it can give.
academy.population.2.title: Workforce: manpower for the army
academy.population.2.body:
Each city has manpower: about {manpowerShare}% of its people can be recruited ({manpowerService}% with mandatory military service). Manpower refills slowly after recruitment. The Ministry of Defence shows your available manpower.

Big cities give big armies; a small country runs out of recruits quickly in a long war.
academy.population.3.title: Public support
academy.population.3.body:
Support (0–100%) is measured in every province; the top bar shows the national average. It starts at {supportStart}% and moves each week toward a target set by:

• GDP growth (+), public services (+), finished buildings in the province (+{buildingSupport} each, up to +{buildingSupportMax}),
• inflation (−), high taxes (−), heavy debt (−), sanctions on you (−), food shortages (−),
• unassimilated or assimilating people (−), rebels next door (−),
• war: being invaded rallies the people (+{defenderRally}); won and lost battles and provinces move support too,
• technology (stability category, +).

The Support map mode shows it province by province.
academy.population.4.title: Conquered people and assimilation
academy.population.4.body:
A conquered province keeps its culture. It produces {unassimilatedPenalty}% less and is less loyal until assimilated. While you are still at war with its people, the province is occupied: it cannot riot and cannot be assimilated. Both become possible after peace.

Assimilation (Ministry of the Interior → Conquered land) costs about {assimilationPerPerson} per person, at least {assimilationMin}, more for culturally distant or rival peoples, and takes {assimilationTurns} weeks. During that time the province is less content. Assimilate all starts every eligible province at once and shows the total cost first.
academy.construction.title: Construction and Infrastructure
academy.construction.1.title: How to build
academy.construction.1.body:
• Open a province and tap Select next to one or more cities (on a PC, Shift-click or Shift-drag to select many).
• The selection bar appears: tap Invest.
• Choose what to build. The dialog shows the price per city, the build time, the total cost and what the budget will look like when it is finished.
• Confirm: the whole price is paid at once from the treasury.

You can select cities in several provinces and order the same building in all of them with one order.
academy.construction.2.title: Buildings, prices and build times
academy.construction.2.body:
Price of the first level, build time, and GDP added per year (as a share of the price):

• Factory: {cost_factory}, {weeks_factory} weeks, {gdp_factory}% a year.
• University: {cost_university}, {weeks_university} weeks, {gdp_university}% a year.
• Agriculture: {cost_agriculture}, {weeks_agriculture} weeks, {gdp_agriculture}% a year.
• Infrastructure: {cost_infrastructure}, {weeks_infrastructure} weeks, {gdp_infrastructure}% a year.
• Energy: {cost_energy}, {weeks_energy} weeks, {gdp_energy}% a year.
• Hospital: {cost_hospital}, {weeks_hospital} weeks, {gdp_hospital}% a year.
• Missile factory: {cost_missileFactory}, {weeks_missileFactory} weeks.
• Drone factory: {cost_droneFactory}, {weeks_droneFactory} weeks.
• Air defense factory: {cost_airDefenseFactory}, {weeks_airDefenseFactory} weeks.
• Military base: {cost_militaryBase}, {weeks_militaryBase} weeks.

Prices follow your country's price level, and the investment-cost technology lowers them.
academy.construction.3.title: Levels and upkeep
academy.construction.3.body:
Several buildings of the same kind in one city are its levels. Each level costs {levelCostGrowth}% more than the one before, and its GDP, upkeep and returns follow what you paid. One order can add up to {maxPerCity} levels per city.

Every building has a yearly upkeep paid by its owner, which shows in the budget as Building upkeep. Check the Budget when finished line in the dialog before you confirm.
academy.construction.4.title: What buildings give
academy.construction.4.body:
• Economic buildings add GDP to the host country when finished (and so more taxes).
• Each finished building raises support in its province (+{buildingSupport}, up to +{buildingSupportMax}).
• Missile, drone and air defense factories let you produce those weapons; more factories produce faster.
• A military base raises the city's base level by one (up to {maxBase}): more recruits per week, special forces from level {specialMinBase}, reservists called up in defense and a defense bonus.
academy.construction.5.title: Following construction
academy.construction.5.body:
The Ministry of Finance lists your projects under Projects with the weeks left. When one finishes, you get a message and the building starts working from that week. A project's price is paid up front, so check your treasury first; building in a city you later lose means the building goes with the city.

Air defense systems are ordered for a city from its province card (Air defense here; you need an air defense factory) and take {adWeeks} weeks for levels 1 / 2 / 3.
academy.military.title: Military
academy.military.1.title: Units
academy.military.1.body:
• Soldiers (regular units): the main army, strength 1 each.
• Special forces: strength {specialStrength} each, but they cost more to recruit and {specialUpkeep}× as much to keep. Only cities with a base of level {specialMinBase} or higher can train them.
• Reservists: they only defend, and only where a base can call them up. They cost {reservistUpkeep}% of a soldier.
• Trainees: soldiers still in training; they help defend their own city at strength {traineeStrength}.
academy.military.2.title: Recruitment
academy.military.2.body:
Select cities (Select in a province), then tap Recruit in the selection bar, or use the Ministry of Defence. Choose the unit, then either a number per city or a percentage of each city's manpower. The dialog shows how many recruits you get, the cost and the training time.

Limits:

• the city's manpower,
• the base level: at most {caps} recruits per week for base levels 0 / 1 / 2 / 3,
• your treasury.
academy.military.3.title: Training time
academy.military.3.body:
• Soldiers: {regularTrain} week. Recruited this week, they join an army next week.
• Special forces: {specialTrain} weeks.

The new soldiers appear as an army in their province. Until then they are trainees; if the city is captured while they train, they are lost.
academy.military.4.title: Military costs
academy.military.4.body: Recruiting costs {regularCostWeeks} weeks of a soldier's upkeep for soldiers and {specialCostWeeks} weeks for special forces, paid at once. After that every soldier costs upkeep every week (Military in the budget). A soldier's cost is set per country so that the starting army costs what the country really spends on defense. Armies at sea cost more. Technology (military upkeep) lowers the bill.
academy.military.5.title: Mandatory military service
academy.military.5.body: In the Ministry of Defence you can introduce or abolish mandatory service. With service, the reserves grow and each city gives more recruits ({manpowerService}% instead of {manpowerShare}% of its people). Introducing it costs {serviceSupport} points of support at once. Without service, the reserves slowly shrink.
academy.military.6.title: Missiles, drones, air defense and nuclear weapons
academy.military.6.body:
• Production: with missile or drone factories, order weapons in the Ministry of Defence (arsenal). More factories mean faster production.
• Strikes: on a city of a country you are at war with, choose missiles or drones in range and launch from a military base. Missiles hit next week; drones fly province by province. Strikes kill soldiers and damage the economy.
• Air defense: levels 1 / 2 / 3 intercept {adIntercept}% of incoming missiles in its range; it needs an air defense factory.
• Nuclear weapons: countries that have them can use them; the damage is devastating and the world answers with sanctions and hatred. Any country can start its own nuclear program in the Ministry of Defence; it costs {nuclearCost} and takes about {nuclearYears} years.
academy.warfare.title: Warfare
academy.warfare.1.title: Declaring war
academy.warfare.1.body: Open a country (tap one of its provinces → Diplomacy) and choose Declare war. The game asks you to confirm. Relations with the target drop sharply, its allies may join it, and your allies may be asked to join you. You cannot declare war on your allies, or on a country with which you signed a non-aggression pact while it lasts.
academy.warfare.2.title: Moving armies
academy.warfare.2.body:
Open the province with your army, tap + next to the army to select it (several can be selected), then open the target province and tap Move here. Armies move one province per week along the shortest path.

You may enter only: enemy land, your allies' land, countries that host your base, or countries that gave you military access. Over the sea, armies travel about {kmPerTurn} km a week; each port gives transport for {transportPerPort} soldiers. Convoys can be intercepted, more often near enemy air defense.
academy.warfare.3.title: Battles
academy.warfare.3.body:
When enemy armies stand in the same province, a battle is fought that week:

• Attack = strength of the attackers × {supplied}% if a neighboring province is yours or an ally's (supplied), or × {cutOff}% if cut off.
• Defense = strength of the defenders, plus reservists the base calls up and trainees, × (1 + {defenderBonus}% + {baseDefense}% per base level).
• Both sides vary by up to ±{randomness}%.

The stronger side wins. The loser loses more; if it had less than {routRatio}% of the winner's strength, it is wiped out. The losing armies retreat if they can.
academy.warfare.4.title: Territory control
academy.warfare.4.body: When the attacker wins, or a province has no defenders, the province changes owner. Its people keep their culture (see Population). A country that loses its last province is conquered and leaves the game. Losing provinces also costs support; capturing them raises it.
academy.warfare.5.title: War score and peace
academy.warfare.5.body: Captured provinces, won battles and strikes build your war score. In the country dialog, Peace talks lets you choose your terms: provinces to keep (each costs points of war score), returning your lost provinces, reparations (up to {maxReparations}% of their GDP), making them a vassal or demilitarizing them. You can send only terms your score covers. Long wars wear both sides out, and the AI accepts peace more readily when it is losing.
academy.warfare.6.title: Consequences of war
academy.warfare.6.body:
• Being invaded rallies your people; losing battles and provinces costs support.
• The world reacts: relations drop with the target's allies, and others may sanction you.
• Investment returns between enemies stop.
• Conquered provinces must be assimilated after peace, or they produce less and can riot.
• Armies cost money every week, and long wars drain the treasury.
academy.diplomacy.title: Diplomacy
academy.diplomacy.1.title: Relations
academy.diplomacy.1.body: Every pair of countries has relations from −100 to +100. They start from history (alliances, rivalries, wars) and move with every action: aid raises them, sanctions, threats and wars lower them, and they slowly drift back over time. The Relations map mode colors the world by what it thinks of you. A country's dialog shows your relations, its leader, alliances, its AI profile and goals, and its opinions of others.
academy.diplomacy.2.title: Diplomatic points
academy.diplomacy.2.body:
Every action abroad costs diplomatic points (Dipl. in the top bar). You earn 1 point a week, plus up to 2 more for a large economy, scaled by your credibility; points stop growing at {pointsCap} weeks' worth.

Costs: improve relations {costImprove}, insult {costInsult}, aid {costAid}, military access {costAccess}, trade request {costDeal}, sanctions {costSanction}, ultimatum {costUltimatum}, military base {costBase}, alliance {costAlliance}, vassal {costVassal}.
academy.diplomacy.3.title: Alliances and pacts
academy.diplomacy.3.body: Propose a defense pact to a friendly country (relations of at least {pactMinRelation} help), or ask to join an existing alliance. Allies may join your wars and you theirs; their armies can cross each other's land. The Alliances map mode shows the blocs.
academy.diplomacy.4.title: Friendly actions
academy.diplomacy.4.body:
• Improve relations: +{improvePerTurn} a week for {improveTurns} weeks (at most {improveMax} at once).
• Aid: send money from your treasury, or missiles and drones.
• Weapons trade: buy from or sell to countries that like you.
• Military access: permission for your armies to cross their land (they can revoke it).
• Military base: ask for or pay for a base in one of their cities.
• Trade request: a package deal (below).
academy.diplomacy.5.title: Pressure
academy.diplomacy.5.body:
• Insult: lowers relations on purpose.
• Sanctions: cut trade and slow their growth; how much depends on how much their economy depends on yours.
• Ultimatum: demand a province, a base, money, leaving an alliance, lifting sanctions or becoming your vassal, and threaten war, sanctions or other steps. They have {ultimatumDeadline} weeks to answer. If they refuse and you do not carry out the threat, your credibility (starting at {credibilityStart}) falls.
• Vassals: a much weaker country can become your vassal; it pays you tribute every week ({vassalTribute}% of its tax income).
academy.diplomacy.6.title: Trade request
academy.diplomacy.6.body:
In a country's dialog, Trade request lets you build a package. Each side can give money (slider), provinces (never the capital), a declaration of war on a third country, joining sanctions against a third country, and military access. Both sides can also sign a defense pact or a non-aggression pact ({nonAggressionYears} years without war between you).

The likelihood meter (very low, low, medium, high) changes as you edit the offer. They accept when what they gain is worth more than what they give, adjusted by relations and by how strong the third country is.
academy.diplomacy.7.title: Requests from others
academy.diplomacy.7.body: AI countries also act: they may ask you to join their wars, send you ultimatums or offer peace. Answers matter: refusing an ally lowers relations; accepting an ultimatum keeps the peace but costs you what they demanded.
academy.politics.title: Politics and Government
academy.politics.1.title: How your government works
academy.politics.1.body: You lead the country as its head (the title follows the real country: president, prime minister, king…). There are no elections in Modern Leader and no choice of political system or ideology: those features are not currently available. Your power rests on one thing: public support.
academy.politics.2.title: Stability: riots
academy.politics.2.body: When support in a province falls below {riotThreshold}%, it riots: you are warned, and the province produces {riotPenalty}% less. The riots end when support climbs back above {riotEnd}%. The Ministry of the Interior lists rioting provinces.
academy.politics.3.title: Revolution and secession
academy.politics.3.body:
A revolution breaks out when national support is below {nationalThreshold}% and provinces holding at least {riotPopShare}% of your people have rioted for {minRiotTurns} weeks or more. Rebels take the angriest provinces (never the capital) and fight for the rest.

• Defeat them: the country survives, but loses {crushedGdpLoss}% of GDP and takes on debt; another revolution cannot start for {calmTurns} weeks.
• Rebels that hold part of the country for {secessionTurns} weeks make it a new, independent country.
• Rebels that take everything win: game over.
academy.politics.4.title: Government decisions
academy.politics.4.body: Your political tools are the decisions in the ministries: taxes, public services and research (Finance), mandatory military service (Defence), assimilation of conquered land (Interior), and every action abroad (Foreign Affairs). Each changes support: see Population and Workforce for the full list of what raises and lowers it.
academy.politics.5.title: Goals
academy.politics.5.body: Your country has goals for the coming years (Menu → Goals), for example growing GDP, keeping inflation low or staying in an alliance. They guide the AI countries too, and following yours is a good way to plan.
academy.advanced.title: Advanced Gameplay
academy.advanced.1.title: Technology
academy.advanced.1.body: Research spending raises your technology level; each level gives {pointsPerLevel} points to assign in the Technology panel (the light bulb). Categories, each with a cap: economic growth, tax collection, military upkeep, investment costs, research, stability and administration. The panel shows the exact effect of each point and how long the next level will take at today's spending.
academy.advanced.2.title: Economic strategy
academy.advanced.2.body:
• Invest early: buildings pay back for the rest of the game, and they raise support where they stand.
• Watch the Budget when finished line: a factory adds GDP, but its upkeep is paid every week.
• Keep debt under {debtThreshold}% of GDP and inflation under {inflationThreshold}%.
• Investing abroad in friendly countries earns returns and builds ties; avoid countries you may fight.
academy.advanced.3.title: Military planning
academy.advanced.3.body:
• Build bases where you recruit: a higher base level allows more recruits per week, special forces and stronger defense.
• Attack from your own or allied land so your armies stay supplied; a cut-off army fights at {cutOff}%.
• The AI attacks when it is clearly stronger; on harder levels it attacks with a smaller edge, so keep a garrison on your borders.
• Empty provinces fall to any enemy army.
• Air defense over your bases and big cities blunts missile strikes.
academy.advanced.4.title: International strategy
academy.advanced.4.body:
• Spend points on relations before you need them: allies join wars only if they like you enough.
• Make threats you can carry out; failed ultimatums cost credibility, and credibility affects your points.
• Sanctions hurt most when the target depends on your trade (the country dialog shows the economic ties both ways).
• Use trade requests to buy what you need: a non-aggression pact on one border lets you move armies to another.
academy.winning.title: Winning and Losing
academy.winning.1.title: Victory
academy.winning.1.body: You win when your country owns every inhabited province in the world. Rankings (the podium) show how you compare along the way: power, GDP, population, army and more.
academy.winning.2.title: Defeat
academy.winning.2.body:
You lose when:

• an enemy takes your last province (conquered), or
• a revolution wins and the rebels take the whole country.

There is no other game over: bankruptcy and debt hurt you through growth, inflation and support, which lead to riots and revolution.
academy.winning.3.title: How to get there
academy.winning.3.body: A strong economy pays for everything else. Grow GDP, keep people content, build bases and an army, make friends, then expand where the world will tolerate it, and assimilate what you take after peace so it produces and stays calm.
academy.winning.4.title: Mistakes to avoid
academy.winning.4.body:
• Printing money again and again: inflation eats growth and support.
• Very high taxes: they slow the economy and push provinces toward riots.
• Ignoring riots: {minRiotTurns} weeks of riots in a large part of the country can start a revolution.
• Leaving borders empty during a war.
• Fighting several strong countries at once.
• Threatening without the means to act: credibility falls.
• Forgetting assimilation after a war.
log.title: History
log.credibility: Our credibility fell: a threat was not carried out.
peace.summary: This treaty: you keep {provinces} provinces ({people} people), {back} of yours come back, they pay {money}.
peace.capitulatedText: No army left and more than half its people lost. You may take all {provinces} provinces it still holds ({people} people) and end the war.
peace.capitulationDone: {country} capitulated. All its land is yours.
peace.notCapitulated: They have not capitulated: they still have an army or most of their people.
foreign.capitulationRequest: {country} demands our capitulation: all our land. Refuse and keep fighting?
goals.rank: Reach #{rank} in the world power ranking
goals.reward: Reward: +{support} support · +{relation} relations with friends · +{tech} technology points · +{points} diplomatic points
event.boom.title: Economic boom
event.boom.text: Exports and investment are up. The windfall can grow the economy further or go to the people.
event.recession.title: Recession
event.recession.text: Orders fall and firms cut jobs. Economists urge action.
event.energyCrisis.title: Energy crisis
event.energyCrisis.text: Gas and power prices have jumped. Households and industry ask for help.
event.protests.title: Protests
event.protests.text: Crowds fill the squares, angry about the cost of living.
event.scandal.title: Government scandal
event.scandal.text: The press has proof that a minister took bribes.
event.strike.title: General strike
event.strike.text: Unions call a nationwide strike over wages.
event.flood.title: Floods
event.flood.text: Rivers burst their banks; towns and roads are under water.
event.drought.title: Drought
event.drought.text: A dry summer ruins the harvest.
event.borderIncident.title: Border incident
event.borderIncident.text: Soldiers from {country} crossed our border and exchanged fire with a patrol.
event.diplomaticCrisis.title: Diplomatic crisis
event.diplomaticCrisis.text: Our ambassador insulted {country} in a leaked recording.
event.breakthrough.title: Scientific breakthrough
event.breakthrough.text: Our researchers made a discovery the world is talking about.
event.warWeariness.title: War weariness
event.warWeariness.text: Families of soldiers ask how long the war will last.
lesson.listHint: Learn by doing: each lesson opens a practice game (never saved), lights up the control to use and checks that you did it.
lesson.unavailable: Lessons open a practice game. Return to the main menu to start one; your campaign is never touched.
lesson.notSaved: This is a practice game: it is not saved.
lesson.basics.title: Basic controls
lesson.basics.1: Tap the money block in the top bar (treasury, GDP, inflation) to open the Ministry of Finance.
lesson.basics.2: Close the panel with the × in its corner.
lesson.basics.3: Tap Support in the top bar: the Ministry of the Interior shows how content your people are.
lesson.basics.4: Press Next Turn. One turn is one week.
lesson.economy.title: Economy and budget
lesson.economy.1: Open the Ministry of Finance (the money block in the top bar).
lesson.economy.2: Move the tax or public services slider and let go. Watch the weekly balance change.
lesson.economy.3: Press Next Turn to see the new budget at work.
lesson.construction.title: Construction
lesson.construction.1: Tap one of your provinces on the map (the highlighted country) to open its card.
lesson.construction.2: Tap Select next to a city.
lesson.construction.3: Tap Invest in the bar at the bottom.
lesson.construction.4: Choose a building and confirm. The price is paid at once; building takes a few weeks.
lesson.technology.title: Technology
lesson.technology.1: Tap the light bulb in the top bar.
lesson.technology.2: Assign a technology point with + next to a category.
lesson.recruitment.title: Recruitment
lesson.recruitment.1: Open one of your provinces and tap Select next to a city.
lesson.recruitment.2: Tap Recruit in the bar at the bottom.
lesson.recruitment.3: Set how many and confirm. Soldiers are ready in one week.
lesson.movement.title: Moving armies
lesson.movement.1: Open a province with your army, tap + next to it, then open a neighboring province of yours and tap Move here.
lesson.movement.2: Press Next Turn: armies move one province a week.
lesson.war.title: War
lesson.war.1: Tap a neighboring country on the map, then its Diplomacy button. (This is only a practice game.)
lesson.peace.title: Peace talks
lesson.peace.1: You need a war first: do the War lesson, or declare war on a neighbor.
lesson.peace.2: Open the country you are at war with (tap it on the map, then Diplomacy).
lesson.peace.3: Tap Peace talks: choose provinces to keep and terms your war score can pay for.
lesson.diplomacy.title: Diplomacy
lesson.diplomacy.1: Tap Dipl. in the top bar: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
lesson.diplomacy.2: Open a country (from the list or the map) to see its dialog.
lesson.diplomacy.3: Tap Improve relations. Every action abroad costs diplomatic points.
lesson.objectives.title: Goals and history
lesson.objectives.1: Tap Menu in the top bar.
lesson.objectives.2: Open Goals: each has a deadline, progress and a reward.
lesson.objectives.3: Open Menu again and then History: the record of your campaign.
